questions.q: Which of these is part of an API's contract?
questions.explain: A contract is what clients can observe and depend on. Internals such as function names and tables can change freely as long as the observable behaviour does not.
options: The names of the functions inside the handler
The request and response schemas for each status code, required headers, the error format and how values such as money and dates are represented
The programming language the server is written in

questions.q: After switching from PGlite to the pg driver, amountKobo starts arriving as "1000000" instead of 1000000. Why does the driver do this?
questions.explain: The driver chooses correctness over convenience. Your mapper must turn the string into the representation your contract promises, checking that it is a safe integer.
options: It is a bug in the driver
A PostgreSQL bigint can exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so the driver returns a string instead of risking a silently wrong number
JSON cannot contain numbers larger than 1,000
PostgreSQL stores all numbers as text

questions.q: Transfer ids may one day exceed 2<sup>53</sup>. How should the contract represent them?
questions.explain: JavaScript clients parse JSON numbers into doubles, which cannot hold every integer above 253. A string keeps the exact digits, and JSON has no BigInt type.
options: As a BigInt in the JSON

questions.q: A handler returns { createdAt: new Date(...) }. What does a JavaScript client get after JSON.parse?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify calls the date's toJSON, producing an ISO string, and JSON.parse leaves it as a string. The contract says "type": "string", "format": "date-time".
options: A string in ISO 8601 format, which the client must parse itself

questions.q: What does { "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Transfer" } mean in an OpenAPI document?
questions.explain: # is the document itself, and the rest is a path into it. Shared schemas are written once under components and referenced wherever they are used.
options: Download the schema from the internet
Use the schema defined at that path inside this same document

questions.q: Why does TransferRequest use additionalProperties: false, while Transfer (the response) does not?
questions.explain: The server controls both schemas but plays different roles: it reads requests (be precise about what you accept) and writes responses (leave room to add fields later).
options: Strict input catches client typos and stops clients setting fields like status; open responses let the server add fields that tolerant clients ignore
OpenAPI only allows it on requests

questions.q: What is the difference between a response field typed ["string", "null"] and required, and a field that is simply not required?
questions.explain: Clients write different code for "always there, maybe null" and "maybe not there". The contract should say which one you mean.
options: None; both mean the value may be absent
The first is always present, sometimes null; the second may be missing from the object entirely
The first is only for requests
The second must always be null

questions.q: What is the main risk when a team keeps a hand-written OpenAPI document and separate hand-written validation code?
questions.explain: Keep one source of truth: generate validation from the document (contract-first) or the document from the code (code-first), and test the running server against it.
options: The two drift apart, so the documentation promises one thing and the server does another

questions.q: What does a provider contract test check?
questions.explain: The provider (the server) is exercised like a client would use it, and each response is validated against the contract. It catches drift such as the pg string amounts before release.
options: That the client parses responses correctly
That the real handler's responses match the schema the contract gives for each returned status code
That the database has the right indexes
That the OpenAPI document is valid YAML

questions.q: A handler returns 500 with { "error": "oops" } for one test case, and the contract does not list 500 for that operation. What should the provider contract test do?
questions.explain: An undocumented status is contract drift too. Either the handler is wrong, or the contract is missing a response that clients need to know about.
options: Pass, because 500 errors are never part of a contract
Fail: the status is not in the contract, so clients have no documented shape to handle
Ignore the body and check only the status

questions.q: What does consumer-driven contract testing add to provider tests?
questions.explain: A document says what exists; consumer expectations say what is used. A field no consumer reads can change freely; one the fraud service reads cannot.
options: Each client records what it actually relies on, so the provider knows who a change breaks, and what is safe to change
It tests the client's user interface
It runs the clients' code on the server

questions.q: You make the optional request field note required. Who breaks?
questions.explain: For requests, the server is the reader. Narrowing what it accepts turns yesterday's valid requests into today's 400s.
options: Nobody; required fields are always safe
Existing clients that do not send note: their requests are now rejected

questions.q: You add "reversed" to the response enum Transfer.status. Why can this break clients?
questions.explain: Widening a response widens what readers must handle. Announce it, document that clients must handle unknown values, or gate it behind a new version.
options: Clients are the readers; code that handles only the values it knew may crash or misbehave on a new one
The server can no longer send "completed"

questions.q: You add "USD" to the enum of the request field currency (which already allowed "NGN"). Is this breaking?
questions.explain: Widening what a reader accepts is safe for writers. The same change on a response enum would be risky, because there the client is the reader.
options: Yes, every enum change is breaking
No: the server accepts more than before, and every old request is still valid
Yes, because old clients will start sending USD
Only if the field is required

questions.q: Which rule summarises safe evolution?
questions.explain: A change is safe when every unchanged old party can still read what the new party writes. Servers read requests and write responses, so the rules are mirror images.
options: Requests may narrow; responses may widen
Requests may widen; responses may narrow (and add fields tolerant readers ignore)
Any change is safe with a new version number in the document

questions.q: You want to rename the response field note to memo without breaking anyone. Which plan works?
questions.explain: Expand, migrate, contract: each step is compatible on its own, and the removal happens only when the evidence (consumer expectations, logs) says nobody depends on the old field.
options: Rename it in one release and update the docs
Return both fields, move clients to memo while watching usage, then remove note (in a new version if anyone may still read it)
Rename it and return 410 to old clients

questions.q: Why is evolving an event schema harder than evolving an HTTP response?
questions.explain: An HTTP response is read once, right away. An event written last year can be read again today by a consumer you have never heard of.
options: Old events stay stored and are replayed, and consumers may be unknown, so consumers must handle every version that still exists
Events are never read more than once

questions.q: Why does every event carry a unique id in its envelope?
questions.explain: Message delivery is at-least-once. The event id lets a consumer skip events it already handled, exactly as the idempotency key did for transfer requests.
options: So consumers can recognise redeliveries and process each event once, like an idempotency key

questions.q: What does an upcaster do?
questions.explain: Stored events are never rewritten. Upcasters translate them on read, one version step at a time, so adding version 3 means writing one new function.
options: Rewrites all stored events to the newest schema in the database
Converts an old version of an event to the next version when a consumer reads it, so one code path handles every version

questions.q: Why should a producer validate an event against its schema before publishing it?
questions.explain: A bad HTTP response affects one request. A bad event is permanent history. Catch it where it is created.
options: An invalid event is stored and replayed forever, affecting every consumer; refusing it at the source contains the damage

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: undefined properties are dropped, NaN becomes null, and a Set has no own enumerable properties, so it becomes {}. None of these throw, which is why they slip past tests.
questions.code:
const order = { id: 7, note: undefined, fee: NaN, tags: new Set(["rent"]), paid: true };
console.log(JSON.stringify(order));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The nearest double to 9007199254740993 is 9007199254740992, so the client silently gets a different id. That is why large ids travel as strings.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify throws a TypeError for BigInt. A replacer can choose a representation, here a string, and the contract must say that is what clients receive.

questions.q: A tiny type check from the validator. What does this print?
questions.explain: A numeric string is not an integer. 10.0 is the same number as 10 in JavaScript, so it is an integer. A type list accepts a value that matches any of its types.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The typo shows up twice, which is the most helpful message a client can get: the field it meant is missing, and the one it sent is unknown.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The reference is a path. Dropping #/ and walking the parts one by one reaches the shared schema.

questions.q: A response schema changes. What does this simplified check print?
questions.explain: Only fields that old clients could read matter, so the loop walks the old schema. fee is new and harmless for tolerant readers; removing note breaks anyone who reads it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Version 1 goes through both upcasters in order; version 2 only through the second. Each upcaster knows only one step, which keeps them small.

questions.q: A consumer expectation is checked against a response. What does this print?
questions.explain: amountKobo is a string, and createdAt is missing, so its type is "undefined". status is not in the consumer's expectations, so it is not checked: this consumer does not care about it.

questions.q: Write validate(schema, value, path = "$") supporting type ("object", "string", "integer"), required, properties, additionalProperties: false and minimum. It returns a list of messages like "$.amountKobo: expected integer", "$.to: is required", "$.x: is not allowed", "$.amountKobo: must be at least 1".
questions.explain: A type mismatch stops the checks for that value (there is no point checking minimum on a string). Every other problem is collected, so the client learns everything in one response.
questions.expected:
[]
[
  '$.to: is required',
  '$.amountKobo: expected integer',
  '$.x: is not allowed'
]
[ '$.amountKobo: must be at least 1' ]
[ '$: expected object' ]

questions.q: Write checkResponse(contract, status, body) that finds the schema for status in contract.responses and checks each property listed in the schema's fields (a map of field to "integer" or "string"). Return "PASS", "FAIL undocumented status N", or "FAIL field1, field2".
questions.explain: Two failure kinds: a documented status with the wrong shape, and a status the contract does not mention at all. Both are drift that clients will trip over.
questions.expected:
PASS
FAIL id, amountKobo
PASS
FAIL undocumented status 500

questions.q: Write requestBreaks(before, after) for request schemas. Report "X became required" for a field that is required in after but not in before (including new required fields), and "X: values A,B no longer accepted" when enum values were removed. Print the result for the starter schemas.
questions.explain: For requests the server is the reader: anything that makes it accept less breaks old clients. A new required field is just a special case of that, while a new optional field would pass.
questions.expected:
[
  'note became required',
  'channel became required',
  'currency: values USD no longer accepted'
]

questions.q: Events of type order.paid exist in versions 1, 2 and 3. Write readLatest(event) that upcasts with the given functions until version 3 and returns the data. Print the result for the three stored events.
questions.explain: Every stored version ends in the same shape, so the rest of the consumer has one code path. The newest events pass through untouched.

questions.q: Write toTransfer(row) mapping a database row to the contract shape: id as a string, amountKobo as a safe integer (accept a number or a string of digits; otherwise throw), and createdAt as an ISO string. Print the results for the two rows, and the error message for the third.
questions.explain: One mapper per resource is where representation is decided. Whatever the driver returns, clients always get the same types, and a value that cannot be represented faithfully fails loudly instead of being rounded.

questions.q: Write publish(type, version, data) that returns an envelope { id, type, version, data } with ids "evt-1", "evt-2" … and throws "invalid event: amountKobo" when data.amountKobo is not a positive integer. Then write a consumer handle(event) that ignores ids it has already processed. Deliver evt-1 twice and print what the consumer does.
questions.explain: The producer guards the schema; the consumer guards against redelivery using the envelope's id. Together they give an event contract that survives both bugs and at-least-once delivery.
questions.expected:
evt-1: SMS for ₦10000
evt-1: duplicate, skipped
invalid event: amountKobo
